entry.summary: 原问题：历史上谐振子的升降算符是怎么发现的？
entry.content:
原问题：历史上谐振子的升降算符是怎么发现的？

刚学格里菲斯，看到谐振子引出升降算符这一块觉得特别不可思议。想知道历史上发现这个的背景，谁发现的？真的是纯粹的注意力惊人吗？

这是我去年在知乎上回答过的一个问题。当时我从经典谐振子的哈密顿方程出发，说明了为什么会自然出现升降算符的形式，并且最后还引入了正则量子化的思路。

最近学了一点量子场论，偶然间翻回了这篇文章，又想到了一些新的话题，因此我将以前的回答与这些整合了一下。

1. 经典谐振子的运动方程​

注意到：海森堡狄拉克等人显然是纯粹的注意力惊人。 因此 Attention is all you need：订阅一个 ChatGPT Plus / Claude Pro 等模型就可以完美解决你的问题（确信）。

但如果我们只是为了在量子力学中自然地引入谐振子的定义的话，其实很简单。我们考虑一维经典谐振子的哈密顿量：

H=p22m+12mω2x2.H=\frac{p^2}{2m}+\frac12m\omega^2x^2.H=2mp2​+21​mω2x2.

正则方程给出一组耦合的一阶微分方程：

x˙=∂H∂p,p˙=−∂H∂x.\dot x=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p}, \qquad \dot p=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial x}.x˙=∂p∂H​,p˙​=−∂x∂H​.

代入哈密顿量：

x˙=pm,p˙=−mω2x.\dot x=\frac{p}{m}, \qquad \dot p=-m\omega^2x.x˙=mp​,p˙​=−mω2x.

一般而言，我们只关心位移 xxx 的参数方程，因此会将后式代入前式，得到一个二阶微分方程。但经典力学学的比较好的同学，会想到相空间与其中的轨迹。因此我们同时考虑 x,px,px,p 的解。定义一个状态向量1：

v=(xp),\boldsymbol v= \begin{pmatrix} x\\p \end{pmatrix},v=(xp​),

于是系统的运动方程就可以写为

dvdt=Mv,\frac{\mathrm d\boldsymbol v}{\mathrm dt}=M\boldsymbol v,dtdv​=Mv,

其中

M=(01/m−mω20).M=\begin{pmatrix} 0&1/m\\ -m\omega^2&0 \end{pmatrix}.M=(0−mω2​1/m0​).

为了将两个变量解耦，我们可以将系数矩阵对角化，这样系数矩阵就会变成简单的对角阵，我们就得到了两个独立的一阶微分方程。

计算：系数矩阵的特征方程为

det⁡(M−λI)=∣−λ1/m−mω2−λ∣=λ2+ω2=0.\det(M-\lambda I) = \begin{vmatrix} -\lambda&1/m\\ -m\omega^2&-\lambda \end{vmatrix} =\lambda^2+\omega^2=0.det(M−λI)=​−λ−mω2​1/m−λ​​=λ2+ω2=0.

得到两个特征值：

λ+=iω,λ−=−iω.\lambda_+=\mathrm i\omega, \qquad \lambda_-=-\mathrm i\omega.λ+​=iω,λ−​=−iω.

对应的特征向量可以选取为

v±=(1±imω).\boldsymbol v_\pm= \begin{pmatrix} 1\\ \pm\mathrm im\omega \end{pmatrix}.v±​=(1±imω​).

原则上，这里特征向量的选取存在一个模长的自由度（复数倍）。通常我们会对其进行归一化。但我们保留这个形式的特征向量，很快我们就能看到原因。

接下来用特征向量构造矩阵 PPP：

P=(11imω−imω),P= \begin{pmatrix} 1&1\\ \mathrm im\omega&-\mathrm im\omega \end{pmatrix},P=(1imω​1−imω​),

顺便计算：

P−1=12mω(mω−imωi).P^{-1}= \frac{1}{2m\omega} \begin{pmatrix} m\omega & -\ii \\ m\omega & \ii \end{pmatrix}.P−1=2mω1​(mωmω​−ii​).

那么根据线性代数的相似对角化，我们就有：

M=PΛP−1,Λ=(iω00−iω).M=P\Lambda P^{-1}, \qquad \Lambda= \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm i\omega&0\\ 0&-\mathrm i\omega \end{pmatrix}.M=PΛP−1,Λ=(iω0​0−iω​).

原来的运动方程可以写成

ddt(P−1v)=Λ(P−1v).\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} (P^{-1}\boldsymbol v) = \Lambda(P^{-1}\boldsymbol v).dtd​(P−1v)=Λ(P−1v).

现在计算：

P−1v=12mω(mωx−ipmωx+ip).P^{-1}\boldsymbol v =\frac{1}{2m\omega} \begin{pmatrix} m\omega x-\ii p\\ m\omega x+\ii p \end{pmatrix}.P−1v=2mω1​(mωx−ipmωx+ip​).

不难发现：格里菲斯书上空降的升降算符定义自然地出现了。我们因此定义：

a=12mω(mωx+ip),a∗=12mω(mωx−ip).a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2m\omega}}(m\omega x+\mathrm ip), \qquad a^*=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2m\omega}}(m\omega x-\mathrm ip).a=2mω​1​(mωx+ip),a∗=2mω​1​(mωx−ip).

原方程组就等价于这个复的一阶微分方程

a˙=−iωa,\dot a=-\mathrm i\omega a,a˙=−iωa,

其一般解为

a(t)=a(0)e−iωt,a(t)=a(0)e^{-\mathrm i\omega t},a(t)=a(0)e−iωt,

将它代回去求解 x(t),p(t)x(t),p(t)x(t),p(t)，就可以重新得到普通谐振子的三角函数解。

然而现在还有一个小问题，我们看一下现在 aaa 的量纲：

kg⋅s−1⋅mkg⋅s−1=m⋅kg⋅s−1,\frac{\text{kg}\cdot \text{s}^{-1} \cdot \text{m}}{\sqrt{\text{kg}\cdot \text{s}^{-1}}} = \text{m} \cdot \sqrt{\text{kg}\cdot \text{s}^{-1}},kg⋅s−1​kg⋅s−1⋅m​=m⋅kg⋅s−1​,

不不不这无疑是诡异的，根本就没有这种量纲！因此我们必须引入一个平衡量纲的常数。而且为了避免新引入的常数的量纲也出现这种问题，我们必须在根号里加入这个常数。注意：

kg⋅s−1⋅mkg⋅s−1⋅m2⋅kg⋅s−1=1,\frac{\text{kg}\cdot \text{s}^{-1} \cdot \text{m}}{\sqrt{\text{kg}\cdot \text{s}^{-1} \cdot \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{kg} \cdot \text{s}^{-1}}} = 1,kg⋅s−1⋅m2⋅kg⋅s−1​kg⋅s−1⋅m​=1,

我们就定义：

a=12ℏmω(mωx+ip),a = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\hbar m\omega}}(m\omega x+\mathrm ip),a=2ℏmω​1​(mωx+ip),

此时 aaa 变成了一个无量纲的函数，而

[ℏ]=m2⋅kg⋅s−1=[S]=[J][\hbar] = \text{m}^2 \cdot \text{kg} \cdot \text{s}^{-1} = [S] = [J][ℏ]=m2⋅kg⋅s−1=[S]=[J]

也就是说 ℏ\hbarℏ 具有作用量（或者角动量）的量纲，非常的简洁优美，隐隐具有作用量的神圣感。更进一步地，注意到：

ℏωa∗a=ℏωm2ω2x2+p22ℏmω=p22m+12mω2x2=H,\hbar \omega a^*a = \hbar \omega \frac{m^2\omega^2 x^2 + p^2}{2\hbar m\omega} = \frac{p^2}{2m} + \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x^2 = H,ℏωa∗a=ℏω2ℏmωm2ω2x2+p2​=2mp2​+21​mω2x2=H,

恰好就是量子力学中的哈密顿量！当然，这里少了一份零点能，这是量子力学的非对易性独有的。而且目前 ℏ\hbarℏ 只是一个平衡量纲用的常数，没有理由把它直接解释成约化普朗克常数。

note

你可能想问为什么是 ℏ\hbarℏ 而不是 hhh，毕竟它们的量纲是相同的。实际上，这是因为我们之前省略了“弧度”这个单位：

[mωx]=kg⋅rad⋅s−1⋅m[m\omega x] = \text{kg} \cdot \text{rad}\cdot \text{s}^{-1} \cdot \text{m}[mωx]=kg⋅rad⋅s−1⋅m

约化普朗克常数的定义实际上就是为了消除掉圆频率的弧度：

ℏ=h2π,[ℏ]=[h]rad\hbar = \frac{h}{2\pi},\qquad [\hbar] = \frac{[h]}{\text{rad}}ℏ=2πh​,[ℏ]=rad[h]​

这样才能保证 ℏω=hf\hbar\omega = hfℏω=hf 是“一份”能量。当然，在标准单位制中弧度是无量纲的，这段论证并不严格，我只是给出一种比较合理的解释而已。

2. 升降“算符”的经典解释​

考虑到大多数学校开设的课程深度，关于哈密顿力学的详细讨论基本上会截止到正则方程、刘维尔定理等处，后面更深层次的理论会讲的非常科普性。所以我们先来复习一下经典力学中的哈密顿-雅可比理论和作用量-角变量方法。这里只讲解一维的体系，因为写起来简单。

正则变换与泊松括号​

经典力学的一个基本技巧就是坐标变换，如果我们能寻找到一组好的坐标，系统的动力学演化通常可以非常简单地求解出来。因此，我们来讨论一下哈密顿力学的坐标变换。我们已经有一组正则坐标 (q,p)(q,p)(q,p)，满足哈密顿方程：

q˙=∂H∂p,p˙=−∂H∂q.\dot q=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p}, \qquad \dot p=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}.q˙​=∂p∂H​,p˙​=−∂q∂H​.

现在考虑更换坐标：

Q=Q(q,p,t),P=P(q,p,t),Q=Q(q,p,t),\qquad P=P(q,p,t),Q=Q(q,p,t),P=P(q,p,t),

有一个很自然的想法：我们希望坐标变换能够让哈密顿方程保持原来的形式。也就是希望存在一个新的哈密顿量 K(Q,P,t)K(Q,P,t)K(Q,P,t)，使得

Q˙=∂K∂P,P˙=−∂K∂Q.\dot Q=\frac{\partial K}{\partial P}, \qquad \dot P=-\frac{\partial K}{\partial Q}.Q˙​=∂P∂K​,P˙=−∂Q∂K​.

满足这个要求的变换，就叫正则变换。

note

你可以理解为：我们期待物理规律不随我们观测世界的方式而发生变化，这也是爱因斯坦建立相对论的出发点。当然，我们这里其实是反过来的：爱因斯坦的做法是从任意坐标变换出发，要求理论不变；我们是要求理论不变，而寻求满足条件的坐标变换。但结果是一样的。

更深层次地，广义相对论相当于认为度规是不变量，在任意光滑坐标变换下其分量取值会变化；而哈密顿力学相当于认为“辛形式”是不变量，在任意正则坐标变换下哈密顿量会发生变化。我们不详细讨论这个了。

那么，问题来了：我们怎么判断一个坐标变换是不是正则的呢？一个很好用的工具就是泊松括号：

{f,g}q,p≡∂f∂q∂g∂p−∂f∂p∂g∂q.\{f, g\}_{q, p} \equiv \frac{\partial f}{\partial q} \frac{\partial g}{\partial p} - \frac{\partial f}{\partial p} \frac{\partial g}{\partial q}.{f,g}q,p​≡∂q∂f​∂p∂g​−∂p∂f​∂q∂g​.

哈密顿-雅可比理论​

我们的出发点相当简单：能不能通过正则变换，找到一组新的正则坐标，让哈密顿方程变得非常简单，甚至完全不需要求解？注意到：

我们的的出发点是周期性运动：这类运动非常的优美且特殊，经过一个周期之后，正则坐标 x,px, px,p 的取值会回到初始条件，在相空间中画出一条闭合的轨迹。很自然地，我们就来考虑这个轨迹围出的面积：

I=12π∫∫ ⁣dx ⁣dpI= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int\int\dd x \dd pI=2π1​∫∫dxdp

我们除了一个 2π2\pi2π，你可以理解为一种归一化。很快你就能明白这个系数的意义。注意根据 Stokes 公式，这个积分还可以写作

I=12π∮p  ⁣dxI = \frac{1}{2\pi}\oint p\,\dd xI=2π1​∮pdx

这里积分的路径就是正则坐标的相空间轨迹。

并取角变量

ϕ=ωt+ϕ0.\phi=\omega t+\phi_0.ϕ=ωt+ϕ0​.

它们满足

{ϕ,I}=1,\{\phi,I\}=1,{ϕ,I}=1,

并且

I˙=0,ϕ˙=ω.\dot I=0, \qquad \dot\phi=\omega.I˙=0,ϕ˙​=ω.

于是经典复变量可以写成

a=Iℏe−iϕ.\boxed{ a=\sqrt{\frac I\hbar}e^{-\mathrm i\phi}. }a=ℏI​​e−iϕ.​

这说明，复变量实际上把谐振子的作用量与角变量组合到了同一个复数中。

对于谐振子，经典相空间中的轨道是椭圆；适当缩放坐标后，它就变成了复平面中的圆周运动。

我们最初通过矩阵对角化得到的

a˙=−iωa\dot a=-\mathrm i\omega aa˙=−iωa

也就不难理解了：它只是复平面上的匀速旋转。

从这个角度看，a,a∗a,a^*a,a∗ 在经典理论中已经拥有自然的动力学意义。量子化只是进一步改变了这些变量的数学性质和物理解释。

三、从泊松括号到升降算符​

考虑经典力学中的泊松括号：

{A,B}=∂A∂x∂B∂p−∂A∂p∂B∂x.\{A,B\} = \frac{\partial A}{\partial x} \frac{\partial B}{\partial p} - \frac{\partial A}{\partial p} \frac{\partial B}{\partial x}.{A,B}=∂x∂A​∂p∂B​−∂p∂A​∂x∂B​.

显然有

{x,p}=1.\{x,p\}=1.{x,p}=1.

对刚才构造的复变量，可以计算：

{a,a∗}=CC∗{mωx+ip, mωx−ip}=−2imω∣C∣2=−iℏ.\begin{aligned} \{a,a^*\} &= C C^* \{m\omega x+\mathrm ip,\, m\omega x-\mathrm ip\}\\ &=-2\mathrm im\omega|C|^2\\ &=-\frac{\mathrm i}{\hbar}. \end{aligned}{a,a∗}​=CC∗{mωx+ip,mωx−ip}=−2imω∣C∣2=−ℏi​.​

狄拉克在早期量子力学的发展中，提出了以泊松括号与量子对易子的对应关系来理解正则量子化的思想：

{A,B}⟶1iℏ[A^,B^].\boxed{ \{A,B\} \longrightarrow \frac{1}{\mathrm i\hbar} [\hat A,\hat B]. }{A,B}⟶iℏ1​[A^,B^].​

这里

[A^,B^]=A^B^−B^A^.[\hat A,\hat B]=\hat A\hat B-\hat B\hat A.[A^,B^]=A^B^−B^A^.

于是经典正则关系对应于

[x^,p^]=iℏ1^.[\hat x,\hat p]=\mathrm i\hbar\hat 1.[x^,p^​]=iℏ1^.

同样，复变量的泊松括号对应于

[a^,a^†]=1^.\boxed{ [\hat a,\hat a^\dagger]=\hat 1. }[a^,a^†]=1^.​

这里 a^†\hat a^\daggera^† 是 a^\hat aa^ 的厄米共轭。

现在，我们终于得到了熟悉的升降算符对易关系。

这个过程也说明了为什么需要选择刚才的归一化系数：我们希望量子化后的复变量满足标准的对易关系。

需要提醒的是，泊松括号与对易子的这种对应不能作为对任意经典函数都严格成立的通用量子化规则。对于这里涉及的线性变量，它是精确的；但对于更一般的函数，还会出现算符排序等问题。

下面考虑海森堡运动方程：

dA^dt=iℏ[H^,A^]+∂A^∂t.\frac{\mathrm d\hat A}{\mathrm dt} = \frac{\mathrm i}{\hbar}[\hat H,\hat A] +\frac{\partial\hat A}{\partial t}.dtdA^​=ℏi​[H^,A^]+∂t∂A^​.

取量子谐振子的哈密顿量：

H^=p^22m+12mω2x^2,\hat H = \frac{\hat p^2}{2m} +\frac12m\omega^2\hat x^2,H^=2mp^​2​+21​mω2x^2,

直接计算便得到

da^dt=−iωa^,da^†dt=iωa^†.\frac{\mathrm d\hat a}{\mathrm dt} =-\mathrm i\omega\hat a, \qquad \frac{\mathrm d\hat a^\dagger}{\mathrm dt} =\mathrm i\omega\hat a^\dagger.dtda^​=−iωa^,dtda^†​=iωa^†.

也可以直接使用海森堡绘景下的演化公式：

至此，我们从经典谐振子的哈密顿方程出发，通过复对角化与正则量子化，得到了量子谐振子升降算符的形式及其运动方程。

但这样的推导还留下了不少问题。

四、重新审视：归一化系数的相位真的无关紧要吗？​

上面的推导只确定了

∣C∣=12ℏmω,|C|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\hbar m\omega}},∣C∣=2ℏmω​1​,

并没有确定其相位。

因此最一般的选择应当是

C=eiθ2ℏmω.C=\frac{e^{\mathrm i\theta}}{\sqrt{2\hbar m\omega}}.C=2ℏmω​eiθ​.

过去我很自然地认为，这个相位可以忽略，因为量子力学不关心全局相位。

但重新考虑以后，我发现这个理由并不充分。

量子力学中，不同量子态之间的相对相位显然具有物理意义。这里对算符引入一个相位，究竟是全局相位，还是可能在不同态之间产生相对相位？

为了区分它们，我们记

a^θ=eiθa^0,a^θ†=e−iθa^0†.\hat a_\theta=e^{\mathrm i\theta}\hat a_0, \qquad \hat a_\theta^\dagger=e^{-\mathrm i\theta}\hat a_0^\dagger.a^θ​=eiθa^0​,a^θ†​=e−iθa^0†​.

首先，

[a^θ,a^θ†]=1,[\hat a_\theta,\hat a_\theta^\dagger]=1,[a^θ​,a^θ†​]=1,

并且

a^θ†a^θ=a^0†a^0.\hat a_\theta^\dagger\hat a_\theta =\hat a_0^\dagger\hat a_0.a^θ†​a^θ​=a^0†​a^0​.

所以这个相位不会改变谐振子的数算符和哈密顿量。

但如果考虑 Fock 态的构造：

∣n⟩θ=(a^θ†)nn!∣0⟩,|n\rangle_\theta = \frac{(\hat a_\theta^\dagger)^n}{\sqrt{n!}} |0\rangle,∣n⟩θ​=n!​(a^θ†​)n​∣0⟩,

就会得到

∣n⟩θ=e−inθ∣n⟩0.\boxed{ |n\rangle_\theta=e^{-\mathrm in\theta}|n\rangle_0. }∣n⟩θ​=e−inθ∣n⟩0​.​

注意，这里的相位依赖于 nnn。

不同能级的基矢获得不同的相位，所以我们不能直接使用“量子态的整体相位不可观测”来解释它。

例如，考虑

因此，追问束缚势的来源，确实可以帮助我们理解某些有效谐振子激发与真实多体系统之间的关系。

但我们仍然不能仅凭一个有效谐振子的哈密顿量，就确定它的激发量子究竟对应什么物理对象。

这还需要考虑完整系统的动力学、相互作用、对称性，以及我们能够实际测量的物理量。

十二、再回头看经典复振幅​

经历这些讨论后，可以重新看待最初从经典谐振子中构造的复变量：

a=mωx+ip2ℏmω.a=\frac{m\omega x+\mathrm ip}{\sqrt{2\hbar m\omega}}.a=2ℏmω​mωx+ip​.

在经典力学中，它表示作用量和相位的组合。

量子化以后，它成为满足玻色型对易关系的算符。

而在量子谐振子中，这个算符还可以与相干态联系起来。

定义相干态 ∣α⟩|\alpha\rangle∣α⟩：

a^∣α⟩=α∣α⟩.\hat a|\alpha\rangle = \alpha|\alpha\rangle.a^∣α⟩=α∣α⟩.

在海森堡绘景中，

a^(t)=a^(0)e−iωt.\hat a(t)=\hat a(0)e^{-\mathrm i\omega t}.a^(t)=a^(0)e−iωt.

因此

⟨α∣a^(t)∣α⟩=αe−iωt.\langle\alpha|\hat a(t)|\alpha\rangle = \alpha e^{-\mathrm i\omega t}.⟨α∣a^(t)∣α⟩=αe−iωt.

这个形式与经典复振幅的演化完全相同。

对谐振子，相干态中位置和动量的期望值也严格遵循经典谐振子的运动方程。

这说明最初通过经典动力学对角化得到的变量，在量子理论中仍然保留了非常明确的经典对应。

从经典相空间的复坐标，到量子谐振子的升降算符，再到量子场的产生湮灭算符，这些结构之间的联系是相当自然的。

但它们的物理意义逐渐发生了变化：

在经典理论中，aaa 描述振幅与相位。

在单粒子量子谐振子中，a^†\hat a^\daggera^† 改变能量本征态。

在一个玻色场的正常模式中，a^†\hat a^\daggera^† 可以产生一个场的量子。

在凝聚态多体系统中，类似的算符又可能描述声子或其他集体激发。

升降算符的代数结构给出了这些描述共同的数学基础；至于究竟升降了什么，则需要回到具体的物理系统中理解。

一点历史补充​

最开始的知乎问题问的是：升降算符究竟是谁发现的？

这和本文讨论的数学重构是两个不同的问题。

1925 年，海森堡建立了矩阵力学，Born、Jordan 等人随后参与完善这一理论。狄拉克也在同年发表了 The Fundamental Equations of Quantum Mechanics，建立起经典泊松括号与量子理论代数结构之间的重要联系。

我们今天熟悉的谐振子代数解法，则是在矩阵力学、算符理论以及后来量子力学教材的整理中逐渐发展形成的。不能简单地把整套方法归结为某个人突然发现了某个算符的形式。

关于谐振子代数解法的具体历史，Rushka 和 Freericks 在 2020 年的一篇文章中进行了专门梳理。

所以，本文最初通过对角化经典动力学矩阵来得到升降算符的方式，主要是一种帮助理解的推导。

它说明了升降算符形式的数学动机，却不应被当成真实的历史发现过程。

Footnotes​

  1. 严格来讲这里是有问题的，x,px, px,p 具有未归一化的量纲，因此状态向量的内积会导致量纲量纲不同的物理量相加。但为了讨论的简便性，我们把量纲的问题统一放到后面处理。 ↩

entry.title: A Tensor Formulation of Linear Algebra
entry.summary: This article explains how to reformulate linear algebra in the index language of tensors, gives a basic introduction to higher-rank tensors, and finally introduces the metric and explains where raising and lowering indices come from. entry.content:
This article explains how to reformulate linear algebra in the index language of tensors, gives a basic introduction to higher-rank tensors, and finally introduces the metric and explains where raising and lowering indices come from. For readers with a solid mathematical background (say, those familiar with the rigorous definitions of dual spaces and inner products), everything here is very trivial, and may be skipped.

We assume a fairly basic familiarity with linear algebra, such as the definitions of a vector space and of a basis, and also some acquaintance with the basic notions of maps, such as injective, surjective and bijective. A few things are not covered in an introductory linear algebra course; for those I will state the basic definitions here, and for more detailed discussions one may consult Linear Algebra Done Right, or any textbook on advanced linear algebra.

1. Linear Algebra​

Vector Spaces​

In linear algebra, a (finite-dimensional) vector space always admits a basis {eμ}\{e_\mu\}{eμ​}, with respect to which any vector can be expanded.

Index conventions

You may be more familiar with i,j,ki,j,ki,j,k as indices, or with writing 1,2,3,…1, 2, 3, \dots1,2,3,… explicitly. In differential geometry, however, Greek letters μ,ν,ρ,…\mu,\nu,\rho,\dotsμ,ν,ρ,… are usually used for vectors and their components. This is only a convention.

In the context of general relativity (four-dimensional spacetime) one usually assumes μ,ν,ρ,⋯=0,1,2,3\mu,\nu,\rho,\dots = 0,1,2,3μ,ν,ρ,⋯=0,1,2,3, where 000 denotes the time component. But out of a strong historical habit, i,j,k,⋯=1,2,3i,j,k,\dots = 1,2,3i,j,k,⋯=1,2,3 is also used for spatial indices.

Ordinary Roman letters (such as a,b,ca,b,ca,b,c) are used as abstract indices: they take no concrete values and only indicate tensor type. This is a somewhat subtle topic, which we will discuss in detail later.

Once a basis has been given, any vector can be expanded as:

v=∑μvμeμ.v = \sum_\mu v^\mu e_\mu.v=μ∑​vμeμ​.

Note that we label the components of a vector with upper indices; this is only a convention in differential geometry. You will find later that this notation makes very good sense.

Einstein Summation Convention​

All of the above is very basic linear algebra. But in differential geometry we often meet operations with summation signs nested inside one another (for instance, contracting the Riemann curvature tensor completely to obtain the Ricci scalar), and writing out every summation sign is undoubtedly intimidating. For this reason we introduce the Einstein summation convention:

Einstein summation convention

In a notation carrying arbitrary indices, when the same letter appears as an upper and as a lower index, it means that this index is summed over. For example:

vμeμ≡∑μvμeμ,v^\mu e_\mu \equiv \sum_\mu v^\mu e_\mu,vμeμ​≡μ∑​vμeμ​,

or:

Aμνvν≡∑νAμνvν.A^\mu{}_\nu v^\nu \equiv \sum_\nu A^\mu{}_\nu v^\nu.Aμν​vν≡ν∑​Aμν​vν.

We need not worry for now about what exactly these symbols mean; it will become clear as we read on. At present we may simply treat all this as a game with symbols.

Physicists usually omit the basis, define a vector directly by its components vμv^\muvμ, and then restrict it by the transformation rule for vector components. That definition may be more intuitive, but it stays somewhat “on the surface”. We use the more mathematical definition here, which is advantageous for finding “invariants” and things that are “canonical”. Concretely, under our definition we want to emphasize:

  1. vμv^\muvμ are the components of the vector vvv in the basis {eμ}\{e_\mu\}{eμ​};
  2. {eμ}\{e_\mu\}{eμ​} is a genuine set of vectors.

Dual Vector Spaces​

We first define dual vectors.

Dual vector

A dual vector is a linear functional defined on a vector space VVV:

ω:V→R,v↦ω(v),\omega: V \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad v \mapsto \omega(v),ω:V→R,v↦ω(v),

satisfying the linearity condition:

ω(αv+βw)=αω(v)+βω(w),∀v,w∈V.\omega(\alpha v+\beta w) = \alpha \omega(v)+\beta \omega(w), \qquad \forall v,w\in V.ω(αv+βw)=αω(v)+βω(w),∀v,w∈V.

If you are more comfortable with matrix language, you may think of it as a row vector.

Addition and scalar multiplication of dual vectors can be defined naturally, so that they genuinely become vectors:

  1. Addition: (ω1+ω2)(v)≡ω1(v)+ω2(v)(\omega_1 + \omega_2)(v) \equiv \omega_1(v) + \omega_2(v)(ω1​+ω2​)(v)≡ω1​(v)+ω2​(v);
  2. Scalar multiplication: (c⋅ω)(v)≡c⋅ω(v)(c \cdot \omega)(v) \equiv c \cdot \omega(v) (c⋅ω)(v)≡c⋅ω(v).

One checks that under these definitions the set of all dual vectors satisfies the definition of a vector space, so they form a new vector space, denoted V∗V^*V∗.

Since dual vectors also form a vector space, we naturally ask what a basis of this space is. Note that if {eμ}\{e_\mu\}{eμ​} is a basis of VVV, we may define the dual basis:

Dual basis

Given a basis {eμ}\{e_\mu\}{eμ​} of VVV, define {eμ}\{e^\mu\}{eμ}1 to be the vectors in V∗V^*V∗ satisfying:

eμ(eν)=δμν.e^\mu(e_\nu)=\delta^\mu{}_\nu.eμ(eν​)=δμν​.

Here δμν\delta^\mu{}_\nuδμν​ is the Kronecker delta:

δμν≡{1,μ=ν,0,μ≠ν.\delta^\mu{}_\nu \equiv \begin{cases} 1, & \mu=\nu,\\ 0, & \mu\neq\nu. \end{cases}δμν​≡{1,0,​μ=ν,μ=ν.​

Differential geometry is used to writing it with one upper and one lower index, so that it can represent the identity matrix.

The Kronecker delta has a very commonly used computational trick: for any (array) vμv^\muvμ one has vμ=vνδμνv^\mu = v^\nu \delta^\mu{}_\nuvμ=vνδμν​; you may expand it to check. Similar conclusions hold for indices of every other type.

Every element ω\omegaω of V∗V^*V∗ can be expanded as a linear combination of {eμ}\{e^\mu\}{eμ}:

ω=ω(eμ)eμ≡ωμeμ.\omega = \omega(e_\mu)e^\mu \equiv \omega_\mu e^\mu.ω=ω(eμ​)eμ≡ωμ​eμ.

Why does this expansion hold? Evaluating both sides on each basis vector eνe_\nueν​, the right-hand side gives ω(eμ)eμ(eν)=ω(eν)\omega(e_\mu)e^\mu(e_\nu)=\omega(e_\nu)ω(eμ​)eμ(eν​)=ω(eν​), the same as the left-hand side. Two linear functionals that agree on a basis agree on the whole space.

And {eμ}\{e^\mu\}{eμ} is linearly independent as well: if cμeμ=0c_\mu e^\mu=0cμ​eμ=0, evaluating on eνe_\nueν​ gives cν=0c_\nu=0cν​=0. Hence the dual basis really is a basis of V∗V^*V∗.

Here again we have used the Einstein summation convention. One sees that vector components are marked with upper indices while dual vector components are marked with lower indices. This convention is not decoration: it corresponds to different transformation laws, and we will see why later.

Evidently, under this definition we may note an important fact: (for finite-dimensional vector spaces) dim⁡V=dim⁡V∗\dim V = \dim V^* dimV=dimV∗.

The Dual of the Dual: Natural Isomorphism​

Since V∗V^*V∗ is a vector space, we can go on to define V∗∗V^{**}V∗∗, the dual of the dual space. But note that V∗∗V^{**}V∗∗ is again a vector space, and we can repeat this nesting indefinitely, which raises our suspicion: is the dual of the dual really necessary? In fact there is a clever way to relate V∗∗V^{**}V∗∗ naturally to VVV:

Natural isomorphism between V∗∗V^{**}V∗∗ and VVV

Note that for any v∈Vv \in Vv∈V we can define a linear functional v′v'v′ on V∗V^*V∗:

v′(ω)≡ω(v),v'(\omega)\equiv\omega(v),v′(ω)≡ω(v),

But a linear functional defined on V∗V^*V∗ is exactly an element of V∗∗V^{**}V∗∗. That is: every vector in VVV corresponds naturally to an element of V∗∗V^{**}V∗∗. In other words:

V≅V∗∗.V \cong V^{**}.V≅V∗∗.

Note that this isomorphism does not depend on the choice of basis; we call it a natural isomorphism, or a canonical isomorphism.

This property allows us to pair vectors and dual vectors naturally:

ω(v)=ωμvμ.\omega(v)=\omega_\mu v^\mu.ω(v)=ωμ​vμ.

Similarly:

v(ω)=vμωμ.v(\omega)=v^\mu\omega_\mu.v(ω)=vμωμ​.

Hence:

ωμvμ=vμωμ.\omega_\mu v^\mu=v^\mu\omega_\mu.ωμ​vμ=vμωμ​.

This looks very trivial, but it illustrates a very important fact: as long as the index structure is correct, we may treat components as ordinary scalars, without thinking about compositions of maps. This is the power of the Einstein summation convention.

If you are unclear about where all these identities come from, write the bases out explicitly and consider the interplay between the basis and the dual basis. Note that components are ordinary real numbers (scalars), and that dual vectors are linear functionals.

On infinite-dimensional spaces

The discussion above is mainly for finite-dimensional vector spaces; in the infinite-dimensional case the matter becomes rather delicate. I have not studied functional analysis systematically myself, so I will not expand on it here. GPT tells me that there are two kinds, the algebraic dual and the continuous dual; interested readers may look them up themselves.

2. Tensors​

Motivation​

Let us first consider the quadratic form so familiar from linear algebra: xTAxx^T A xxTAx. There is nothing mysterious about this expression; we can simply expand it into a sum over components. But if we forget matrices for a moment and put our attention back on the vector space itself, what mathematical object does it actually describe?

Here xxx is a column vector, and after transposition xTx^TxT is a row vector2. Or, in the language of tensors, they are a vector and a dual vector respectively. And the whole quadratic form xTAxx^T A xxTAx is a real number. More generally, we now allow the two sides of a “quadratic form” to take different vectors: that is, consider the object xTAyx^T A yxTAy. Then we may regard the matrix as a map sending a dual vector and a vector to a real number:

A:V∗×V→R,A(xT,y)≡xTAy,A: V^* \times V \to \R, \qquad A(x^T, y) \equiv x^T A y,A:V∗×V→R,A(xT,y)≡xTAy,

where the product sign between two vector spaces denotes the Cartesian product:

Cartesian product

The Cartesian product is simply putting the elements of two vector spaces together3 to form an ordered pair:

V×W≡{(v,w)∣v∈V,w∈W}.V \times W \equiv \{(v, w)\mid v \in V, w \in W\}.V×W≡{(v,w)∣v∈V,w∈W}.

Note that “ordered” means we cannot exchange the order at will; in general (v,w)≠(w,v)(v, w) \neq (w, v)(v,w)=(w,v). In particular, for the Cartesian product of a vector space with itself we use a power notation as shorthand (this is also the origin of the notation Rn\R^nRn we usually use):

Vn≡V×V×⋯×V⏟n copies.V^n \equiv \underbrace{V \times V \times \cdots \times V}_{n\text{ copies}}.Vn≡n copiesV×V×⋯×V​​.

The Cartesian product has some basic properties: the Cartesian product of two vector spaces is again a vector space, the Cartesian product of two subspaces of a vector space is isomorphic to their external direct sum, and so on. We will not give a more detailed introduction and discussion here.

Moreover, we can see that the matrix is linear in each of its two arguments:

(αxT+βyT)Az=αxTAz+βyTAz,xTA(αy+βz)=αxTAy+βxTAz.(\alpha x^T + \beta y^T)Az = \alpha x^TAz + \beta y^TAz, \qquad x^TA(\alpha y + \beta z) = \alpha x^TAy + \beta x^TAz.(αxT+βyT)Az=αxTAz+βyTAz,xTA(αy+βz)=αxTAy+βxTAz.

The discussion above looks very trivial, but it suggests a more general understanding of matrices: a matrix can represent a bilinear map4. At this point we can consider some more general situations.

Tensors​

Let us first define bilinear maps rigorously, or more generally multilinear maps: let V1,V2,⋯ ,VnV_1, V_2, \cdots, V_nV1​,V2​,⋯,Vn​ all be vector spaces defined over R\RR (they may be over another field, but it must be the same one), then an nnn-fold linear map is defined as:

T:V1×V2×⋯×Vn→R,T(v1,v2,⋯ ,vn)=c∈R,T: V_1 \times V_2 \times \cdots \times V_n \to \R, \qquad T(v_1, v_2, \cdots, v_n) = c \in \R,T:V1​×V2​×⋯×Vn​→R,T(v1​,v2​,⋯,vn​)=c∈R,

and for ∀ vi,wi∈Vi, i=1,2,⋯ ,n; α,β∈R\forall \ v_i, w_i \in V_i,\ i = 1, 2, \cdots, n; \ \alpha, \beta \in \R∀ vi​,wi​∈Vi​, i=1,2,⋯,n; α,β∈R, it satisfies:

T(⋯ ,αvi+βwi,⋯ )=αT(⋯ ,vi,⋯ )+βT(⋯ ,wi,⋯ ).T(\cdots, \alpha v_i + \beta w_i, \cdots) = \alpha T(\cdots, v_i, \cdots) + \beta T(\cdots, w_i, \cdots).T(⋯,αvi​+βwi​,⋯)=αT(⋯,vi​,⋯)+βT(⋯,wi​,⋯).

Next we can define tensors in a simple way:

Tensor

A tensor of type (k,l)(k, l)(k,l) is a multilinear map defined on V∗k×Vl{V^*}^k \times V^lV∗k×Vl. In other words, a tensor of type (k,l)(k, l)(k,l) is a multilinear map that linearly maps kkk dual vectors and lll vectors to a real number.

A dual vector maps a vector to a real number, while a vector can map a dual vector to a real number; hence, according to our definition of tensors, they may be called a tensor of type (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1) and a tensor of type (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0) respectively. In particular, we call a scalar (real number) a tensor of type (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0).

From the definition above, we can define addition and scalar multiplication of tensors in a very natural way:

  1. (T+S)(ω1,⋯ ,ωk;v1,⋯ ,vl)≡T(ω1,⋯ ,ωk;v1,⋯ ,vl)+S(ω1,⋯ ,ωk;v1,⋯ ,vl),(T+S)(\omega^1, \cdots, \omega^k; v_1, \cdots, v_l) \equiv T(\omega^1, \cdots, \omega^k; v_1, \cdots, v_l) +S(\omega^1, \cdots, \omega^k; v_1, \cdots, v_l),(T+S)(ω1,⋯,ωk;v1​,⋯,vl​)≡T(ω1,⋯,ωk;v1​,⋯,vl​)+S(ω1,⋯,ωk;v1​,⋯,vl​),
  2. (αT)(ω1,⋯ ,ωk;v1,⋯ ,vl)≡α⋅T(ω1,⋯ ,ωk;v1,⋯ ,vl).(\alpha T)(\omega^1, \cdots, \omega^k; v_1, \cdots, v_l) \equiv \alpha \cdot T(\omega^1, \cdots, \omega^k; v_1, \cdots, v_l).(αT)(ω1,⋯,ωk;v1​,⋯,vl​)≡α⋅T(ω1,⋯,ωk;v1​,⋯,vl​).

Note that this definition requires that only tensors of the same type can be added to or subtracted from one another. This is natural as well; after all, there is no way to define the sum of a matrix and a vector.

Tensor space

Under the addition and scalar multiplication defined above, all tensors of type (k,l)(k, l)(k,l) naturally form a vector space, denoted TV(k,l)\mathscr{T}_V(k, l)TV​(k,l). There is also the notation Tlk\mathscr{T}^k_lTlk​, which omits the base space VVV. A more mathematical notation is Mult⁡((V∗)k×Vl,R)\operatorname{Mult}((V^*)^k \times V^l, \R)Mult((V∗)k×Vl,R), where Mult⁡\operatorname{Mult}Mult stands for multilinear.

Tensor Product​

As with the definition of tensors themselves, the motivation for defining the tensor product is clear: note that under the definition of matrix multiplication, xyTxy^TxyT turns a row vector and a column vector into a matrix; in other words, the tensor product of a (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0)-tensor and a (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1)-tensor is a (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1)-tensor. At the same time, we also notice that:

zT(xyT)w=(zTx)(yTw)∈R,z^T(xy^T)w= (z^Tx)(y^T w) \in \R,zT(xyT)w=(zTx)(yTw)∈R,

That is, this (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1)-tensor acts on a vector and a dual vector by acting with the original two lower-rank tensors separately to get real numbers, and then multiplying them. This suggests the following formal definition:

Tensor product

Let TTT be a (k,l)(k, l)(k,l)-tensor and SSS a (k′,l′)(k', l')(k′,l′)-tensor; then their tensor product is a (k+k′,l+l′)(k+k', l+l')(k+k′,l+l′)-tensor, that is, the multilinear map

T⊗S:V∗k+k′×Vl+l′→R,T \otimes S : {V^*}^{k+k'} \times V^{l+l'} \to \R,T⊗S:V∗k+k′×Vl+l′→R,

whose values are defined by:

(T⊗S)(ω1,⋯ ,ωk,ωk+1,⋯ ,ωk+k′;v1,⋯ ,vl,vl+1,⋯ ,vl+l′)≡ T(ω1,⋯ ,ωk;v1,⋯ ,vl)⋅S(ωk+1,⋯ ,ωk+k′;vl+1,⋯ ,vl+l′).\begin{aligned} &(T \otimes S)(\omega^1, \cdots, \omega^k, \omega^{k+1}, \cdots, \omega^{k+k'}; v_1, \cdots, v_l, v_{l+1}, \cdots, v_{l+l'})\\ \equiv \ &T(\omega^1, \cdots, \omega^k; v_1, \cdots, v_l) \cdot S(\omega^{k+1}, \cdots, \omega^{k+k'}; v_{l+1}, \cdots, v_{l+l'}). \end{aligned}≡ ​(T⊗S)(ω1,⋯,ωk,ωk+1,⋯,ωk+k′;v1​,⋯,vl​,vl+1​,⋯,vl+l′​)T(ω1,⋯,ωk;v1​,⋯,vl​)⋅S(ωk+1,⋯,ωk+k′;vl+1​,⋯,vl+l′​).​

This definition looks frighteningly long, but what it actually says is very trivial: feed the first group of dual vectors and vectors to TTT, and the second group to SSS, then simply multiply the two resulting real numbers. When the remaining inputs are fixed, each input occurs in only one factor, so the resulting map is indeed multilinear.

Addition and scalar multiplication between tensors obtained by tensor products are natural, because what the tensor product gives is nothing but a new tensor, and addition and scalar multiplication of tensors were defined long ago. In particular, from the definition above we also obtain:

(T+T′)⊗S=T⊗S+T′⊗S,T⊗(S+S′)=T⊗S+T⊗S′,α(T⊗S)=(αT)⊗S=T⊗(αS).\begin{aligned} &(T+T')\otimes S=T\otimes S+T'\otimes S,\\ &T\otimes(S+S')=T\otimes S+T\otimes S',\\ &\alpha(T\otimes S)=(\alpha T)\otimes S=T\otimes(\alpha S). \end{aligned}​(T+T′)⊗S=T⊗S+T′⊗S,T⊗(S+S′)=T⊗S+T⊗S′,α(T⊗S)=(αT)⊗S=T⊗(αS).​

That is, the tensor product, as an operation on two tensors, is bilinear. This is natural as well, because on each fixed group of inputs the right-hand side is nothing but a product of two real numbers. Likewise, associativity of multiplication of real numbers guarantees that the tensor product is associative, so parentheses may be omitted when several factors are multiplied.

However, the tensor product in general does not satisfy commutativity. This is because we have fixed the order of the dual-vector inputs and the vector inputs; exchanging two tensors usually changes which inputs each of them receives. For example, when dim⁡V≥2\dim V\geq 2dimV≥2,

(e1⊗e2)(e1,e2)=1,(e2⊗e1)(e1,e2)=0.(e_1\otimes e_2)(e^1,e^2)=1,\qquad (e_2\otimes e_1)(e^1,e^2)=0.(e1​⊗e2​)(e1,e2)=1,(e2​⊗e1​)(e1,e2)=0.

There is a special example here: the tensor product of a dual vector and a vector can be exchanged. This is because we agreed to put all dual-vector inputs in front and all vector inputs at the back; each of them has only one object to map, so exchanging the order in which these two factors are written still gives the same bilinear map. Written out concretely, for v∈Vv\in Vv∈V and ω∈V∗\omega\in V^*ω∈V∗ we have

(v⊗ω)(η;u)=η(v)ω(u),(v\otimes\omega)(\eta;u)=\eta(v)\omega(u),(v⊗ω)(η;u)=η(v)ω(u),

as well as

(ω⊗v)(η;u)=ω(u)η(v).(\omega\otimes v)(\eta;u)=\omega(u)\eta(v).(ω⊗v)(η;u)=ω(u)η(v).

4. The Metric and Raising and Lowering Indices​

The inner product is in fact a very important topic, although it is usually not mentioned deliberately, because the inner product on Rn\R^nRn is too natural. In the language of tensors we use a metric to describe this inner product structure.

Inner Product, Dirac Notation and Duality​

Most elementary linear algebra courses do not introduce the inner product rigorously, so let us first give a rigorous definition of the inner product. Here we temporarily consider a complex vector space VVV.

Let VVV be a vector space over the field of complex numbers C\mathbb{C}C. An inner product on VVV is a map

  1. Linearity: ⟨u,αv+βw⟩=α⟨u,v⟩+β⟨u,w⟩\langle u, \alpha v + \beta w\rangle = \alpha\langle u, v\rangle + \beta\langle u, w\rangle⟨u,αv+βw⟩=α⟨u,v⟩+β⟨u,w⟩;

Now back to the main line of this article. An inner product on a real vector space is just that on a complex vector space with the conjugation removed. Hence the inner product we want to consider maps two vectors symmetrically and bilinearly to a real number, and this happens to be exactly the definition of a special (0,2)(0,2)(0,2)-tensor. We therefore define the metric:

A metric on a real vector space VVV is a (0,2)(0,2)(0,2)-tensor ggg, that is, a bilinear map

g:V×V→R,g: V\times V \to \R,g:V×V→R,

  1. Symmetry: g(u,v)=g(v,u)g(u,v)=g(v,u)g(u,v)=g(v,u);
  2. Non-degeneracy: if some uuu satisfies g(u,v)=0g(u,v)=0g(u,v)=0 for all v∈Vv\in Vv∈V, then necessarily u=0u=0u=0.

Since the metric itself is a (0,2)(0,2)(0,2)-tensor, by the discussion above it can of course be expanded in the dual basis. Choose a basis {eμ}\{e_\mu\}{eμ​} of VVV, with corresponding dual basis {eμ}\{e^\mu\}{eμ}; then

g=gμνeμ⊗eν,gμν≡g(eμ,eν).g=g_{\mu\nu}e^\mu\otimes e^\nu, \qquad g_{\mu\nu}\equiv g(e_\mu,e_\nu).g=gμν​eμ⊗eν,gμν​≡g(eμ​,eν​).

The two most commonly used examples are as follows.

Euclidean metric: in an orthonormal basis its components are

gμν=δμν=diag⁡(1,1,…,1),g_{\mu\nu}=\delta_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,\dots,1),gμν​=δμν​=diag(1,1,…,1),

The Kronecker delta δμν\delta^\mu{}_\nuδμν​ is the component of the identity map. The identity map is canonically defined, and in any basis its components are always diag⁡(1,1,…,1)\operatorname{diag}(1,1,\dots,1)diag(1,1,…,1).

The Euclidean metric, by contrast, is an independently specified symmetric positive-definite (0,2)(0,2)(0,2)-tensor. It does not need the Minkowski metric in order to be defined, nor can it be conjured up out of nothing by “lowering an index” on δμν\delta^\mu{}_\nuδμν​. In an orthonormal basis, gμν=δμνg_{\mu\nu}=\delta_{\mu\nu}gμν​=δμν​ only means that the two sets of components coincide numerically; change the basis, and the metric itself has not changed, yet the components need not still be the identity matrix. For example, the two-dimensional Euclidean plane in the coordinate basis of polar coordinates has gμν=diag⁡(1,r2)g_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{diag}(1,r^2)gμν​=diag(1,r2) (r>0r>0r>0).

Later we will discuss the “raising” and “lowering” of indices. The identity gμρδρν=gμνg_{\mu\rho}\delta^\rho{}_\nu=g_{\mu\nu}gμρ​δρν​=gμν​ certainly holds, but it has already used the metric ggg in advance, so it cannot be taken as a definition that constructs the metric. If all you have learned is general relativity, it is easy to tie the metric together with the Minkowski metric; the Euclidean metric exists independently in the first place.

Minkowski metric: in the coordinate basis of a standard inertial frame its components are

gμν=ημν=diag⁡(−1,1,1,1),g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1),gμν​=ημν​=diag(−1,1,1,1),

Hence

g(u,v)=−u0v0+u1v1+u2v2+u3v3.g(u,v)=-u^0v^0+u^1v^1+u^2v^2+u^3v^3.g(u,v)=−u0v0+u1v1+u2v2+u3v3.

The spacetime interval is exactly this metric acting on infinitesimal displacements:

ds2=ημν dxμdxν=−dt2+dx2+dy2+dz2.\mathrm{d} s^2=\eta_{\mu\nu}\,\mathrm{d} x^\mu \mathrm{d} x^\nu =-\mathrm{d} t^2+\mathrm{d} x^2+\mathrm{d} y^2+\mathrm{d} z^2.ds2=ημν​dxμdxν=−dt2+dx2+dy2+dz2.

Here we have already passed from a fixed vector space to the tangent space chosen according to position on a manifold. In the language of the coordinate basis, the metric is written as

g=gμν dxμ⊗dxν,g=g_{\mu\nu}\,\mathrm{d}x^\mu\otimes\mathrm{d}x^\nu,g=gμν​dxμ⊗dxν,

where dxμ\mathrm{d}x^\mudxμ is the coordinate cotangent basis, and in the Minkowski case the components are the ημν\eta_{\mu\nu}ημν​ above. And ds2\mathrm{d}s^2ds2 is the notation for the line element, which may also be understood as the notation for the quadratic form obtained by letting the metric act on an infinitesimal displacement; it is in fact not a differential (form). For a more detailed discussion please refer to my differential geometry notes (which have not got that far yet, but some day ()

Since g00=−1g_{00}=-1g00​=−1, the contribution of the time direction carries a minus sign; this one sign is precisely the most essential difference between an indefinite metric and the Euclidean metric, and also the source of the fact that “squared length” can be negative in Minkowski spacetime.

note

The gμνg_{\mu\nu}gμν​ written above are all constant matrices, which holds only in Cartesian coordinates (in the Minkowski case, inertial frames). In a general coordinate system gμνg_{\mu\nu}gμν​ is a function of the coordinates.

In particular, in general relativity the metric is no longer a constant matrix given in advance, but a dynamical field gμν(x)g_{\mu\nu}(x)gμν​(x) on spacetime, determined by the distribution of matter through the Einstein field equations together with given boundary conditions and symmetries:

Gμν=8πG Tμν(c=1)G_{\mu\nu}=8\pi G\,T_{\mu\nu} \qquad (c=1)Gμν​=8πGTμν​(c=1)

Hence there exist very many kinds of metrics in general relativity: the gravitational field outside a star, a black hole, an expanding universe, each corresponding to a different gμνg_{\mu\nu}gμν​. Given a metric, one is given a symmetric non-degenerate bilinear structure, and hence a geometry.

The Musical Isomorphism and Raising and Lowering Indices​

Before we discussed the metric, we already knew that vectors and dual vectors are two different kinds of object. Although for a finite-dimensional vector space VVV and V∗V^*V∗ have the same dimension, this does not give a canonical isomorphism. Now that we have a metric, things are different.

Consider a vector v∈Vv\in Vv∈V. If we fix the first argument of the metric and allow only the second to vary, we obtain a map g(v,⋅):V→Rg(v,\cdot):V\to\mathbb Rg(v,⋅):V→R. Since the metric is bilinear, this is plainly a linear functional, that is, an element of V∗V^*V∗. Hence, through the metric, we can make any vector correspond to a dual vector:

♭:V⟶V∗,v⟼g(v,⋅).\begin{aligned} \flat:V&\longrightarrow V^*,\\ v&\longmapsto g(v,\cdot). \end{aligned}♭:Vv​⟶V∗,⟼g(v,⋅).​

This is the insertion we mentioned earlier. Moreover, since the metric is symmetric, it does not matter into which input the insertion is made. The result of ♭(v)\flat(v)♭(v) acting on any w∈Vw\in Vw∈V is

♭(v)(w)=g(v,w).\flat(v)(w)=g(v,w).♭(v)(w)=g(v,w).

This construction requires no choice of basis at all. The bilinearity of the metric also guarantees that ♭\flat♭ itself is a linear map.

Is this map an isomorphism, then? If ♭(v)=0\flat(v)=0♭(v)=0, then g(v,w)=0g(v,w)=0g(v,w)=0 for all w∈Vw\in Vw∈V, and non-degeneracy immediately gives v=0v=0v=0. So ♭\flat♭ is injective; and since the space here is finite-dimensional with dim⁡V=dim⁡V∗\dim V=\dim V^*dimV=dimV∗, it is also surjective. We thus obtain an isomorphism, together with its inverse map:

♭:V→∼V∗,♯=♭−1:V∗→V.\flat:V\xrightarrow{\sim}V^*, \qquad \sharp=\flat^{-1}:V^*\to V.♭:V∼​V∗,♯=♭−1:V∗→V.

This pair of isomorphisms is called the musical isomorphism; the name comes from notational habit: the flat sign ♭\flat♭ lowers the pitch, and the sharp sign ♯\sharp♯ does the opposite. Up to here we have not used any indices. So where on earth do those familiar index-raising and index-lowering formulas in physics textbooks come from?

Let us now choose a basis {eμ}\{e_\mu\}{eμ​} of VVV, together with the corresponding dual basis {eμ}\{e^\mu\}{eμ}. First consider the action of ♭\flat♭ on a basis vector. By definition, ♭(eμ)=g(eμ,⋅)\flat(e_\mu)=g(e_\mu,\cdot)♭(eμ​)=g(eμ​,⋅). This is a dual vector, so it can be expanded in the dual basis. Noticing that

♭(eμ)(eν)=g(eμ,eν)=gμν,\flat(e_\mu)(e_\nu)=g(e_\mu,e_\nu)=g_{\mu\nu},♭(eμ​)(eν​)=g(eμ​,eν​)=gμν​,

we have

♭(eμ)=gμνeν.\flat(e_\mu)=g_{\mu\nu}e^\nu.♭(eμ​)=gμν​eν.

This is now clear: the metric maps a basis vector to a linear combination of the dual basis. For an arbitrary vector v=vμeμv=v^\mu e_\muv=vμeμ​, using linearity:

♭(v)=♭(vμeμ)=vμ♭(eμ)=vμgμνeν.\flat(v)=\flat(v^\mu e_\mu)=v^\mu\flat(e_\mu)=v^\mu g_{\mu\nu}e^\nu.♭(v)=♭(vμeμ​)=vμ♭(eμ​)=vμgμν​eν.

On the other hand, since ♭(v)∈V∗\flat(v)\in V^*♭(v)∈V∗, we can of course write it as ♭(v)=(♭v)νeν\flat(v)=(\flat v)_\nu e^\nu♭(v)=(♭v)ν​eν. Comparing coefficients and using the symmetry of the metric, we obtain

(♭v)ν=gνμvμ.(\flat v)_\nu=g_{\nu\mu}v^\mu.(♭v)ν​=gνμ​vμ.

So the so-called “lowering of indices” is in fact just the component expression of the musical isomorphism ♭\flat♭ in a chosen basis. We defined only one map, and raising and lowering of indices appeared naturally.

Raising indices is the same. Let gμνg^{\mu\nu}gμν be the components of the inverse matrix of the matrix gμνg_{\mu\nu}gμν​, satisfying

gμρgρν=δμν.g^{\mu\rho}g_{\rho\nu}=\delta^\mu{}_\nu.gμρgρν​=δμν​.

This inverse matrix is also symmetric. Compute ♭\flat♭ once:

♭(gμνeν)=gμν♭(eν)=gμνgνρeρ=eμ.\begin{aligned} \flat(g^{\mu\nu}e_\nu) &=g^{\mu\nu}\flat(e_\nu)\\ &=g^{\mu\nu}g_{\nu\rho}e^\rho\\ &=e^\mu. \end{aligned}♭(gμνeν​)​=gμν♭(eν​)=gμνgνρ​eρ=eμ.​

Since ♯=♭−1\sharp=\flat^{-1}♯=♭−1, we therefore have

♯(eμ)=gμνeν.\sharp(e^\mu)=g^{\mu\nu}e_\nu.♯(eμ)=gμνeν​.

For an arbitrary dual vector ω=ωμeμ\omega=\omega_\mu e^\muω=ωμ​eμ, then

♯(ω)=ωμgμνeν=(♯ω)νeν,(♯ω)ν=gνμωμ.\sharp(\omega)=\omega_\mu g^{\mu\nu}e_\nu =(\sharp\omega)^\nu e_\nu, \qquad (\sharp\omega)^\nu=g^{\nu\mu}\omega_\mu.♯(ω)=ωμ​gμνeν​=(♯ω)νeν​,(♯ω)ν=gνμωμ​.

Physics textbooks usually write (♭v)μ(\flat v)_\mu(♭v)μ​ directly as vμv_\muvμ​ and (♯ω)μ(\sharp\omega)^\mu(♯ω)μ as ωμ\omega^\muωμ; that is, with the help of the musical isomorphism they keep the same letter for a vector and its corresponding dual vector. In this way the familiar formulas are

vμ=gμνvν,ωμ=gμνων.v_\mu=g_{\mu\nu}v^\nu, \qquad \omega^\mu=g^{\mu\nu}\omega_\nu.vμ​=gμν​vν,ωμ=gμνων​.

However, v=vμeμv=v^\mu e_\muv=vμeμ​ and ♭(v)=vμeμ\flat(v)=v_\mu e^\mu♭(v)=vμ​eμ are still objects in different spaces; this is especially easy to forget once the basis is omitted, and it is best to be careful about this.

The same can be done for higher-rank tensors. For example, for a (2,0)(2,0)(2,0)-tensor

T=Tμνeμ⊗eν,T=T^{\mu\nu}e_\mu\otimes e_\nu,T=Tμνeμ​⊗eν​,

we let ♭\flat♭ act only on the second tensor factor:

(id⊗♭)(T)=Tμνeμ⊗♭(eν)=Tμνgνρeμ⊗eρ.\begin{aligned} (\mathrm{id}\otimes\flat)(T) &=T^{\mu\nu}e_\mu\otimes\flat(e_\nu)\\ &=T^{\mu\nu}g_{\nu\rho}e_\mu\otimes e^\rho. \end{aligned}(id⊗♭)(T)​=Tμνeμ​⊗♭(eν​)=Tμνgνρ​eμ​⊗eρ.​

Here we have used the tensor product of operators, which in fact means “act on the corresponding spaces separately”; it is used a great deal in quantum computing, and we will not expand on it in detail here. In short, we have thus obtained a (1,1)(1,1)(1,1)-tensor. If its components still use the letter TTT, the expansion is

(id⊗♭)(T)=Tμρeμ⊗eρ,Tμρ=Tμνgνρ.(\mathrm{id}\otimes\flat)(T)=T^\mu{}_\rho e_\mu\otimes e^\rho, \qquad T^\mu{}_\rho=T^{\mu\nu}g_{\nu\rho}.(id⊗♭)(T)=Tμρ​eμ​⊗eρ,Tμρ​=Tμνgνρ​.

For an arbitrary higher-rank tensor, one need only choose the corresponding tensor factor and let ♭\flat♭ or ♯\sharp♯ act on it. This may also be understood equivalently as first taking the tensor product with the metric (with the inverse metric when raising indices), and then contracting one pair of indices.

With raising and lowering of indices, we can also give meaning to a “contraction” between two upper indices: first lower one of the indices with the metric, then do the original contraction. For example

g(v,v)=gμνvμvν=vμvμ=vνvνg(v,v)=g_{\mu\nu}v^\mu v^\nu=v^\mu v_\mu=v_\nu v^\nug(v,v)=gμν​vμvν=vμvμ​=vν​vν

is the “squared length” of the vector vvv, a scalar independent of the choice of basis.

Another example: in the standard inertial coordinate basis of Minkowski spacetime, the four-momentum is written p=pμeμp=p^\mu e_\mup=pμeμ​, with corresponding dual vector ♭(p)=pμeμ\flat(p)=p_\mu e^\mu♭(p)=pμ​eμ. Its norm

pμpμ=ημνpμpν=−E2+∣p⃗∣2p^\mu p_\mu=\eta_{\mu\nu}p^\mu p^\nu=-E^2+|\vec p|^2pμpμ​=ημν​pμpν=−E2+∣p​∣2

is such an invariant, equal to −m2-m^2−m2 (with c=1c=1c=1); this relation is the so-called “mass-shell condition”.

Looks familiar, doesn't it? This is very similar to the earlier idea of mapping a ket to a bra: fixing one variable of the inner product also gave a linear functional. However, the complex inner product is conjugate-linear in the first variable, so the Riesz map u↦φuu\mapsto\varphi_uu↦φu​ there is a conjugate-linear bijection, and cannot directly be taken as the linear isomorphism ♭\flat♭ on the real vector space here. In the real case, they are the same only if the metric is positive-definite.

The construction of ♭\flat♭ depends on the metric itself; change the metric, and ♭\flat♭ changes with it. So V≅V∗V\cong V^*V≅V∗ is not independent of any choice the way the finite-dimensional V≅V∗∗V\cong V^{**}V≅V∗∗ above was; it is natural only after a metric has been given. In other words, V≅V∗∗V\cong V^{**}V≅V∗∗ is the canonical isomorphism in abstract vector spaces that needs no additional structure, whereas V≅V∗V\cong V^*V≅V∗ needs the extra structure of a metric.

Without specifying a metric, vectors and dual vectors are two different kinds of object, and upper and lower indices cannot be moved around at will; this is exactly why we had to distinguish contravariance from covariance earlier.

Lorentz Transformation​

The place where raising and lowering of indices is used most in physics is the Lorentz transformation, that is, a change of basis that preserves the Minkowski metric; in the language of physics, it is those transformations between inertial frames that keep the spacetime interval ds2\mathrm{d}s^2ds2 invariant. This is also why we used the letter Λ\LambdaΛ when discussing changes of basis earlier.

The metric is a (0,2)(0,2)(0,2)-tensor; by the transformation rule discussed in Chapter 3, after a change of basis its components become ΛρμΛσνηρσ\Lambda^\rho{}_\mu\Lambda^\sigma{}_\nu\eta_{\rho\sigma}Λρμ​Λσν​ηρσ​. And requiring the metric to be unchanged means

ΛρμΛσνηρσ=ημν,\Lambda^\rho{}_\mu\Lambda^\sigma{}_\nu\eta_{\rho\sigma}=\eta_{\mu\nu},Λρμ​Λσν​ηρσ​=ημν​,

or, written in matrix language: ΛTηΛ=η\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\etaΛTηΛ=η. Multiplying ΛTηΛ=η\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\etaΛTηΛ=η on the left by (ΛT)−1(\Lambda^T)^{-1}(ΛT)−1 and on the right by η−1\eta^{-1}η−1, we have ηΛη−1=(Λ−1)T\eta\Lambda\eta^{-1}=(\Lambda^{-1})^TηΛη−1=(Λ−1)T; written in indices this is

ηνρΛρσησμ=(Λ−1)μν.\eta_{\nu\rho}\Lambda^\rho{}_\sigma\eta^{\sigma\mu}=(\Lambda^{-1})^\mu{}_\nu.ηνρ​Λρσ​ησμ=(Λ−1)μν​.

The left-hand side is exactly “lowering the first index of Λ\LambdaΛ and raising the second”, that is, written as Λνμ\Lambda_\nu{}^\muΛν​μ. Since the two are equal, physics books simply keep the same letter and directly agree that swapping an index up or down denotes the inverse matrix:

Λνμ≡(Λ−1)μν.\Lambda_\nu{}^\mu \equiv (\Lambda^{-1})^\mu{}_\nu.Λν​μ≡(Λ−1)μν​.

In this way the four transformation rules above can be written in exactly the same shape:

fμ=Λνμeν,fμ=Λνμeν,f_\mu = \Lambda^\nu{}_\mu e_\nu, \qquad f^\mu = \Lambda_\nu{}^\mu e^\nu,fμ​=Λνμ​eν​,fμ=Λν​μeν, ω~μ=Λνμων,v~μ=Λνμvν.\widetilde\omega_\mu = \Lambda^\nu{}_\mu \omega_\nu, \qquad \widetilde v^\mu = \Lambda_\nu{}^\mu v^\nu.ωμ​=Λνμ​ων​,vμ=Λν​μvν.

The difference between upper and lower indices now shows only in the position of the indices on Λ\LambdaΛ, and the defining relation of the inverse matrix has also become a pure index pairing: ΛμνΛμρ=δνρ\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu\Lambda_\mu{}^\rho=\delta^\rho_\nuΛμν​Λμ​ρ=δνρ​. This is why Λ−1\Lambda^{-1}Λ−1 is almost never seen in physics books. This convention depends on the condition of preserving the metric. Under a general change of basis, ηνρΛρσησμ\eta_{\nu\rho}\Lambda^\rho{}_\sigma\eta^{\sigma\mu}ηνρ​Λρσ​ησμ equals neither Λμν\Lambda^\mu{}_\nuΛμν​ nor (Λ−1)μν(\Lambda^{-1})^\mu{}_\nu(Λ−1)μν​; exchanging an index and taking the inverse can be interchanged only for metric-preserving transformations such as Lorentz transformations.

Footnotes​

  1. Many linear algebra textbooks write the dual basis as eμ∗e_\mu^*eμ∗​, but differential geometry usually writes eμe^\mueμ directly, which is more natural later when handling tensors. ↩

  2. It is in fact not rigorous to regard the row vector xTx^TxT directly as a dual vector; this is only a consequence of the fact that the Rn\R^nRn we consider has a natural basis and that one usually chooses the Euclidean inner product (metric). We use this notation for the moment, and return to this question in the last part. ↩

  3. In fact the Cartesian product can be defined for arbitrary sets, and does not necessarily require vector spaces, because an ordered pair does not require the set to have any properties. ↩

  4. Of course, we all know that a matrix can be used to represent a linear map between two vector spaces, or a transformation between two bases; we will discuss this question in the next part. ↩

  5. This is in fact a somewhat delicate question: strictly speaking, after exchanging the order they are not the same; we will return to this point later when discussing the universal property, especially the exchange isomorphism τ\tauτ. ↩

  6. Strictly speaking, one should not use ≡\equiv≡ (defined as) here, but ≅\cong≅ (isomorphic). We discuss this where we discuss the universal property. ↩ ↩2

  7. Strictly speaking, this first definition does involve the question of which tensor product is taken first, but whatever the order, there exists a natural isomorphism between them. However, here we define tensors directly by means of multilinear maps, so this definition is unambiguous: it corresponds to arranging the groups of inputs in order. ↩

  8. This is in fact consistent with our earlier definition: taking W=V∗W=V^*W=V∗ and handling the second input with V∗∗≅VV^{**}\cong VV∗∗≅V, we return to the original v⊗ωv\otimes\omegav⊗ω. ↩

  9. In fact the letter Λ\LambdaΛ is often used to refer to a more special transformation: the Lorentz transformation, which keeps the Minkowski spacetime interval ds2\mathrm{d}s^2ds2 invariant between inertial frames. Of course, we impose no such restriction here. ↩

  10. The inverse of a matrix, in tensor language, is the tensor satisfying Λμρ(Λ−1)ρν=δμν\Lambda^\mu{}_\rho(\Lambda^{-1})^\rho{}_\nu=\delta^\mu{}_\nuΛμρ​(Λ−1)ρν​=δμν​. ↩

  11. Many physics books in fact take this as the definition of a tensor: a (k,l)(k,l)(k,l)-tensor is a set of numbers satisfying the transformation law above, without considering changes of basis. ↩

entry.content:
This is a review of Modern Optics from the Spring 2026 semester, taught by Professor Dai Ya'nan, with reference to Hecht's Optics (5th Edition).

This is an exam-focused review: it only covers the key topics mentioned in Professor Dai's review lectures, and many derivations that I find obvious have been omitted. For a systematic study of optics, consulting a textbook is still recommended.

I don't particularly recommend reading Hecht directly — its sign conventions are highly complex, sometimes even self-contradictory, and much of the content is unnecessary. It reads more like a popular science book than a textbook.

Chapters 1 and 2 are too simple and are omitted.

Chapter 3: Electromagnetic Theory, Photons, and Light​

3.1 Basic Definitions​

Irradiance​

Irradiance III is the average energy transported by an electromagnetic wave per unit area per unit time. For a harmonic wave in vacuum, the magnitude of the time-averaged Poynting vector is the irradiance (unit: W/m2\mathrm{W/m^2}W/m2):

I=⟨S⟩T=c2ϵ0 ∣E⃗0×B⃗0∣  ⟨cos⁡2(k⃗⋅r⃗−ωt)⟩=c2ϵ02 ∣E⃗0×B⃗0∣I = \langle S \rangle_{T} = c^{2}\epsilon_{0}\,|\vec{E}_{0}\times \vec{B}_{0}|\;\langle \cos^{2}(\vec{k}\cdot \vec{r} -\omega t)\rangle = \frac{c^{2}\epsilon_{0}}{2}\,|\vec{E}_{0}\times \vec{B}_{0}|I=⟨S⟩T​=c2ϵ0​∣E0​×B0​∣⟨cos2(k⋅r−ωt)⟩=2c2ϵ0​​∣E0​×B0​∣

In vacuum, ∣B⃗0∣=∣E⃗0∣/c|\vec{B}_{0}| = |\vec{E}_{0}|/c∣B0​∣=∣E0​∣/c, so the irradiance is proportional to the square of the electric field amplitude:

I=⟨S⟩T=c ϵ02 E02I = \langle S \rangle_{T} = \frac{c\,\epsilon_{0}}{2}\,E_{0}^{2}I=⟨S⟩T​=2cϵ0​​E02​

The power PPP (in watts) passing through an area AAA is

P=IA[W=J/s]P = IA \qquad [\mathrm{W} = \mathrm{J/s}]P=IA[W=J/s]

Spherical Waves​

A point source in a homogeneous medium radiates spherical waves. From the scalar wave equation:

E(r,t)=(Ar)cos⁡(kr∓ωt)E(r,t) = \left(\frac{\mathcal{A}}{r}\right)\cos(kr \mp \omega t)E(r,t)=(rA​)cos(kr∓ωt)

where A\mathcal{A}A is the source strength. At any distance rrr, rE0(r)=constrE_0(r) = \text{const}rE0​(r)=const. Thus the amplitude decreases inversely with rrr, and the irradiance of a point source follows the inverse-square law:

I∝1r2.I \propto \frac{1}{r^{2}}.I∝r21​.

Note that spherical electromagnetic waves do not actually exist in reality. This is because Gauss's law ∇⋅E⃗=ρϵ\nabla \cdot \vec{E} = \dfrac{\rho}{\epsilon}∇⋅E=ϵρ​ forcibly erases all differences in charge distribution — it is impossible to construct a charge distribution and motion that produces a spherical wave. Of course, it remains an excellent approximation.

Photon Flux​

For a quasi-monochromatic beam of cross-sectional area AAA, the average photon flux (photons per second) is

Φ=AIhν0\Phi = \frac{AI}{h\nu_0}Φ=hν0​AI​

A single photon carries energy E=hνE = h\nuE=hν (hhh is Planck's constant). Numerically, a P=1P = 1P=1 mW He–Ne laser (λ=632.8  nm\lambda = 632.8\;\mathrm{nm}λ=632.8nm) emits approximately Φ≈3.2×1015\Phi \approx 3.2 \times 10^{15}Φ≈3.2×1015 photons per second.

Radiation Pressure​

Maxwell showed that electromagnetic radiation carries momentum. The instantaneous radiation pressure equals the energy density:

Pr=uE+uB=S(t)cP_r = u_E + u_B = \frac{S(t)}{c}Pr​=uE​+uB​=cS(t)​

The average radiation pressure on a perfectly absorbing surface is

⟨Pr⟩=⟨S(t)⟩c=Ic\langle P_r \rangle = \frac{\langle S(t) \rangle}{c} = \frac{I}{c}⟨Pr​⟩=c⟨S(t)⟩​=cI​

Unit: [Pr]=W m−2/m s−1=N m−2 (pascals)[P_r] = \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}} / \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} = \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}} \,(\text{pascals})[Pr​]=Wm−2/ms−1=Nm−2(pascals).

The force on an absorbing area AAA is F=APrF = AP_rF=APr​. Assuming the volume density of electromagnetic momentum is pvp_vpv​, we have:

F=pv⋅cΔtAΔt,F = \frac{p_v \cdot c\Delta t A}{\Delta t},F=Δtpv​⋅cΔtA​,

Solving simultaneously yields:

pv=Sc2p_v = \frac{S}{c^2}pv​=c2S​

In the photon picture, each quantum carries momentum

p=Ec=hλ=ℏkp = \frac{E}{c} = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \hbar kp=cE​=λh​=ℏk

3.2 Light in Matter​

In a medium with no free charges or currents, that is homogeneous, isotropic, and has linear constitutive relations, Maxwell's equations reduce to:

∇2E⃗=μϵ∂E⃗∂t,∇2B⃗=μϵ∂B⃗∂t,\nabla^2 \vec{E} = \mu \epsilon \frac{\partial{\vec{E}}}{\partial t}, \qquad \nabla^2 \vec{B} = \mu \epsilon \frac{\partial{\vec{B}}}{\partial t},∇2E=μϵ∂t∂E​,∇2B=μϵ∂t∂B​,

These are classical wave equations, with traveling wave solutions:

9.4 Interferometers (Michelson)​

The Michelson interferometer splits a light beam, sends the two parts along different paths, and then recombines them. A compensating plate (identical to the beam splitter) ensures that both beams pass through the same thickness of glass, balancing dispersion so that white-light fringes can be observed. The fringe pattern can reveal optical path differences as small as a fraction of a wavelength, making the Michelson interferometer an extremely sensitive measurement tool.
